Sorry, as much as I enjoy the Linux environment, I don't know much about keeping things tidy. Package managers are nice but the clean-up scripts are only as good as the people who make them. (Windows is just as bad, if not worse. Removal of a program is usually an afterthought for the developers.)

Ideally, all of your important stuff should be on a /home partition. This makes nuking everything else quite trivial. Of course there's always the issue re-installing everything and then configuring it properly. Takes a bit of time but can be worth the restoration of sanity.

The grass is a lot greener once you realize that DEs and their tooling are more or less graphical masturbation and are more or less just for people that don't want to learn about their system. Sure it can help you do stuff if you don't know, but the more you learn about yourself the more the specifications become clear on what exactly you want it to do.

Do a clean install, choose a window manager (you seem to like fluxbox), and learn how to to the basic stuff from terminal, and then start using useful programs not "play with a desktop metaphore". nmtui for network management from command line, dmenu or keybinds for application launcher, and that should be most of it.

Theres some papers on "captive UIs" and the likes, and its really quite intresting. Summed up, the less fancy the UI the less distracted and less mental work it takes to do things and switch between things. I can attest to this, as using i3wm I use no desktop UI, no i3bar, demu, wallpaper, or even window borders. At most the little tabs when it tabbed mode. And I can say is that I have more resources and screen space for my useful programs, and end up less distracted.

If you're really willing to go that far, check out the Surf Browser by Suckless. Its simply a front end for webkit. No menubar, URL bar (unless using dmenu), etc. Just click a link and go somewhere. No tabs, just spawn a new instance. Killing an instance and spawning a new instance with a search engine/homepage open is many times faster than going to the URL bar and typing in duckduckgo in the URL bar.

At the very most the UI is the menu you get on right click, which at most is about 6 items.

Clean, lean, fast system. The Majority of the time CLI/Terminal is the fastest and best interface for programs. /bin/bash is my file manager.

It'll also really help when you go to stuff like Debian testing. When people say stuff breaks, its more often than naught, the large monolithic bloated programs. Like gnome or KDE.
